messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Coast Guard
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi Patel is an 80-year-old widower who spent much of his adult life working with the Coast Guard, a role he still speaks of with pride even now that he is retired. He came to treatment after years of carrying a private burden that began with an accident at sea when he was younger, a moment he still describes indirectly because he cannot bear to name it too plainly. During an operation in a natural coastal area, with water, wind, and open shore all around him, something went wrong and he accidentally caused a serious injury to another person. The details do not come to him in a smooth, orderly way. When he tries to talk about that day, Ravi’s account breaks into disconnected pieces: the sound of motion on the water, a flash of the shoreline, a sudden shift in urgency, then a sense that the scene is gone before he can hold it together. He has said that when he deliberately tries to remember, the harder he reaches for it, the less he can access. At other times, especially when the memory breaks through on its own, it does not feel distant or past at all. It comes back as if he is there again, with all his senses crowded together at once, and the vividness leaves him unsettled and silent.

In the years that followed, Ravi began to notice that certain situations pulled him back toward that day. Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, especially near water or in open outdoor settings, could turn a normal outing into a tense, watchful experience. He has also found that talking about the future is unexpectedly difficult, because any discussion of plans or what might come next presses him into a state of unease he does not fully know how to explain. Even ordinary sirens can jolt him; he stiffens when an ambulance passes and listens until the sound fades, as if something urgent and irreversible might be unfolding again just out of sight. Over time, he developed habits aimed at keeping the memory at a distance. He tells himself that the event did not really happen, or that it was not that bad, even when another part of him knows the seriousness of what occurred. He forces himself toward positive thoughts and tries to push the whole thing out of his mind, but the effort often leaves him drained and more alone with it afterward.

Ravi’s way of moving through the world has narrowed. He avoids unfamiliar places because he cannot assess the danger in them, and he prefers settings where he knows exactly where the exits are and where he can see what is happening around him. In restaurants, waiting rooms, or community gatherings, he always chooses a seat based on how safe or protected he feels, usually with his back to a wall or near a clear path out. Even in retirement, he still carries himself as though he must stay alert to every shift in the environment. He has described feeling that he has to be on guard all the time, and this stance shows up in how carefully he scans spaces before settling in. At other times he has taken more risks than he would admit to others, almost as if testing whether danger will find him anyway. These choices have made his days smaller and more restricted, and they have also made social outings less spontaneous, since he needs time to assess any place before he can tolerate being in it.

Ravi’s understanding of himself has grown harsher over the years. He has come to believe that there is something wrong with him as a person, and that the accident says something enduring about his character. Rather than seeing the event as a terrible mistake in an overwhelming moment, he has often interpreted it as evidence of the sort of man he is. That belief has sat beside the fact that he was widowed, and now, living without his wife’s steady presence, he has had fewer opportunities to speak openly about what he carries. He still functions independently, but his world feels increasingly arranged around caution, silence, and control.

He sought help now because the burden has remained heavy into old age, and because the memories, the sirens, the questions about the future, and the uneasiness in natural settings have become harder to contain. What he most hopes for is some relief from the sense that he must stay on guard forever, and what he most fears is that the event will continue to define who he is until the end of his life.
